definition: The only stock exchange in Nepal. Every listed share, mutual fund unit and debenture trades here. With just one venue, there is no second market to sell on when buyers disappear.
example: Like a town with one haat bazaar: if the bazaar is quiet, there is nowhere else to sell your buffalo.

definition: The main number that tracks the overall price level of listed shares, with bigger companies counting for more. It fell about 43%, from 3,198.60 on 18 August 2021 to 1,815.13 on 25 September 2022.
example: A thermometer for the whole market, not for any one share.

definition: An index for one group of companies only, such as banking, hydropower or life insurance. It shows whether a sector is rising or falling as a whole.
Share price × number of shares. It is what the market says the whole company is worth today.
example: A bank with 20 crore shares at Rs 500 has a market cap of Rs 100 arba.

definition: A firm licensed by SEBON to place buy and sell orders on NEPSE for you. You open a broker account and trade through the broker's TMS.

The broker's online system where your buy and sell orders actually reach NEPSE. Each licensed broker runs its own TMS. It is separate from MeroShare: orders go through TMS, while applications, EDIS approvals and holdings live in MeroShare.

CDSC's website and app for investors. You use it to apply for IPOs, FPOs and rights shares, approve EDIS when you sell, and see your holdings. It is not a place to buy or sell: that happens in your broker's TMS.
Nepal's central depository. It holds every listed share in electronic form, runs MeroShare, and settles trades: it moves the shares and the money after a deal is agreed.
example: If NEPSE is the bazaar where the price is agreed, CDSC is the land office that records the change of owner.

definition: The account that holds your shares electronically, the way a bank account holds your money. You need one to buy or hold any NEPSE share.
The bank or broker that opens and runs your demat account on CDSC's system. Most banks and many brokers act as one.
The 16-digit number that identifies your demat account in CDSC's records. Your shares are held against it, and CDSC allows one IPO application per BOID per issue.

The approval a seller gives in MeroShare to release sold shares from the demat account. Forgetting it is a common and costly mistake: the sale is agreed but settlement fails, and the seller pays a penalty.
Shares and money change hands two working days after the trade. If you buy on Sunday, the shares reach your demat account on Tuesday.
The step after a trade in which the shares actually move to the buyer and the money to the seller. On NEPSE it happens on T+2, through CDSC.
An order with a price limit: the highest price you will pay when buying, or the lowest you will accept when selling. It protects you from paying far more than you meant to in a thin market.
example: Telling the shopkeeper 'I will pay up to Rs 500, not a rupee more.'

definition: The list of buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) waiting at different prices for one share. In a thin share it may hold only a handful of orders.
The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering right now; the ask is the lowest price a seller will accept. A trade happens when they meet.

The gap between the best buying and best selling prices. In thin NEPSE shares it can be Rs 5, Rs 20 or more, sometimes several percent of the price. Buying at the ask and later selling at the bid loses the spread straight away.
example: Like the gap between what a money changer pays for your dollars and what he charges for them.

definition: How many shares are waiting to be bought or sold near the best prices. A deep book can absorb a large order; a shallow one moves sharply when you sell.
A short period before normal trading in which orders are collected to help set the opening price.

The most a share's price may move in one day. For ordinary shares in the normal market it is 15% from the previous close, since 20 April 2026. At the upper circuit you cannot buy higher that day; at the lower circuit you cannot sell lower.

A share that keeps hitting its circuit limit day after day while very few shares change hands. When it turns, it can hit the lower limit day after day and you cannot sell at all. A fast rise on real news is not a trap by itself; the warning is limit hits plus tiny turnover plus a rumour.
example: A one-way bridge: easy to cross in, impossible to cross back when traffic turns.

definition: The rupee value of a share traded on a normal day, averaged over a period such as six months. The Canon Score uses it to grade how easily a share trades.

The average amount of a share that changes hands each day, counted in shares or, as this book usually does, in rupees, over a recent window such as 20 trading days. It tells you how big an order the market can take.
example: Asking for a taxi in a village versus central Kathmandu: five people at once is a problem in the village, trivial in the city.

definition: This book's limit on position size: hold no more of a share than you could sell in 5 trading days while being only 10% of each day's trading. In simple maths, about half of one day's average turnover.
example: A share trading Rs 20 lakh a day allows about Rs 10 lakh; one trading Rs 1 lakh a day allows only about Rs 50,000.

definition: How easily you can sell a share for cash without pushing its price down. In NEPSE it is the most important risk after the business itself. (The same word also describes how much spare money banks have; see Liquidity regime.)
example: A road busy on festival days can be empty when you need a ride.

definition: The risk that you cannot sell when you need to, or only at a much lower price. It is highest exactly when markets fall and buyers vanish.

The share of a company's stock that ordinary investors can actually trade. It leaves out promoter, government and other strategic holdings, cross-holdings and locked-in shares. Chapter 64 gives 5 points at 40% or more, 3 at 25–40%, 1 at 10–25% and 0 below 10%.
example: What matters is not how much water is underground but how much you can draw from the well.

definition: A free float so small that a few orders can move the price a lot. Thin-float shares are prone to circuit traps however good the business.
The date by which you must be a registered shareholder to receive a declared dividend, bonus or rights. Because of T+2, you must buy early enough for the trade to settle before that date.
After the book closure for a bonus or rights issue, the share's price is adjusted downward to reflect the extra shares. The company is not worth less; its value is spread across more shares.
example: Cutting the same roti into more pieces.

definition: The fee your broker charges on each buy and sell, as a percentage that falls for bigger trades: 0.36% up to Rs 50,000 (minimum Rs 10), then lower rates for larger amounts, as of November 2026.
A small regulatory fee of 0.015% of the trade value, paid on each buy and sell.
A fixed charge of about Rs 25 per company per day when shares leave your demat account on a sale. On small trades it is a large share of the cost.
The total cost of buying and later selling: commission and SEBON fee both ways plus the DP charge, before capital gains tax. On a Rs 6,000 position it is about Rs 70, or 1.2%.
A loan to buy shares, secured on those shares. If prices fall far enough, the lender sells your shares, often at the worst time. This book says no margin loans for beginners.
example: Like a family house mortgaged to a moneylender: you live there, but someone else can take it.

definition: A lender's demand for more money when the shares behind a margin loan fall in value. If you cannot pay, the lender sells. In 2021–22 margin calls forced many Nepali investors to sell near the bottom.
Nepali market slang for a person or group that pushes a share's price up through coordinated buying and rumours, then sells to late buyers. Thin-float shares are the usual targets.
A bull market is a long, broad rise in prices; a bear market a long, broad fall. NEPSE's 2021 peak and the fall that followed are the book's main example.
A SEBON-licensed firm that manages share issues (IPOs, FPOs, rights) for companies, and often also acts as share registrar or runs mutual funds.
The firm that keeps a company's list of shareholders up to date and handles allotments, dividends and bonus credits.
A share of ownership in a company. It gives you a part of the profits (through dividends) and a vote at the AGM, and it is paid last if the company fails.
example: Owning one share of a bank is like owning a tiny slice of the whole bank, not a deposit in it.

definition: The nominal value printed on a share, usually Rs 100 for NEPSE companies. Dividends and bonus percentages are quoted on face value, not on the market price.
example: A 20% cash dividend on a Rs 100 face-value share is Rs 20, even if the share trades at Rs 600.

definition: The total face value of the shares a company has issued and been paid for. NRB and other regulators set minimum paid-up capital for some sectors, which is one reason companies issue bonus or rights shares.
A company's first sale of shares to the public, after which it lists on NEPSE. Applications go through ASBA or MeroShare; when demand is higher than the shares on offer, allotment is by lottery.
A sale of new shares to the public by a company that is already listed.

The system for applying to IPOs, FPOs and rights issues. Your bank blocks the amount in your own account instead of taking it; it is released if you get nothing and debited only if you are allotted shares.
A way to set an IPO price. Institutional investors bid within a price band; the price at which enough bids arrive becomes the cut-off, and the public then applies at a fixed discount to it.
example: An auction among wholesale buyers, after which retail customers get the same goods slightly cheaper.

definition: In book building, the price at which enough institutional bids arrive to sell the shares on offer.
When investors apply for more shares than are on offer. Popular NEPSE IPOs are oversubscribed many times, so shares are allotted by lottery.
Parts of some IPOs set aside for particular groups, such as people affected by a hydropower project or Nepalis working abroad. They change who can apply, not what the company is worth.
An offer letting existing shareholders buy new shares, usually below the market price, in proportion to what they already hold. Unlike a bonus issue, you must put in fresh cash.
To give up, or sell, your right to buy rights shares instead of using it yourself.
Rights shares that existing shareholders did not take up. The company can then sell them to others, often by auction.
The price a share should trade at just after a rights issue, once the cheap new shares are blended in. A Rs 400 share with one Rs 100 rights share for each held gives TERP = (400 + 100) ÷ 2 = Rs 250.

Free extra shares given to existing shareholders out of the company's reserves. You hold more shares, but not more of the company, and EPS falls because the same profit is shared across more shares. A 5% tax applies, usually paid by a small cash dividend that exists only for that.
example: Cutting the same roti into more pieces.

definition: Profit paid to shareholders in money. Only real cash dividends count as 'paid' in the Canon Score; a token cash amount that only covers the bonus tax does not.
A listed corporate bond: a loan to a company that pays fixed interest (the coupon) and returns the principal at maturity. Debenture holders are paid before shareholders if the company fails.
The fixed yearly interest a bond or debenture pays, as a percentage of its face value.
The return a bond gives if you buy it at today's price and hold it to the end. When bond prices fall, yields rise, and the other way round.
example: Like a seesaw: price on one side, yield on the other.

definition: A short-term loan to the Government of Nepal, sold by NRB at auction. It is about as safe as a rupee investment gets, and its rate is a guide to short-term interest rates.

full: Citizens and Foreign Employment Savings Bonds
definition: Bonds the government sells to ordinary savers, including Citizens Savings Bonds and Foreign Employment Savings Bonds for Nepalis working abroad.
Money placed in a bank for a fixed period at a fixed rate. It suits emergency money and money waiting to be invested; check the penalty for breaking it early.
A pool of money from many investors, managed by a licensed fund manager and invested in many shares and bonds. You own units of the pool, not the shares directly.
A mutual fund that issues new units and buys them back from you at close to their NAV, so you do not need a buyer on NEPSE to get out.
A mutual fund with a fixed number of units that trade on NEPSE like shares. Their price often sits below the NAV per unit.
What one unit of a mutual fund is worth: the value of everything the fund holds, minus what it owes, divided by the number of units.
Putting a fixed amount into a mutual fund every month, whatever the market does. You buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
example: Planting the kitchen garden every season, rain or no rain.

definition: A period after listing during which some shares, typically promoter shares, may not be sold. When it ends, a wave of newly sellable shares can arrive.
Nepal's central bank. It sets monetary policy, licenses and supervises banks and financial institutions, and manages the currency and foreign exchange reserves.
NRB's decisions on interest rates, bank liquidity and credit, meant to keep prices and the economy stable. Its effects flow through bank lending into NEPSE.
NRB's yearly policy announcement, made early in the fiscal year (around Shrawan), with mid-year reviews. Markets watch it for changes to rates and lending rules.
The repeated swing between easy bank lending and tight bank lending. This book's central idea is that NEPSE moves strongly with it, through bank money, more than through company profits alone.
example: Like the monsoon and the dry season: easy money fills the fields, tight money dries them.

definition: The state of Nepal's banking money at a given time: loose, when banks have spare money and lend easily, or tight, when they are short of loanable funds. Chapter 0.3 sorts it into four phases.
Banks lend freely and money is easy. In this book's plan you may use up to 100% of your active part, never more, and never raise a margin loan in a rally.
Banks run short of money and rates rise. The plan cuts the active part to about half, selling the weakest scores first, and repays margin loans.
Rates are high and the market is beaten down. The plan rebuilds from 50% toward 75%, buying only scores of 70 or more at low prices.
Money starts flowing again. The plan rebuilds toward 100% in half-steps.

This book's working definition: system credit growth above 20%, or the system CD ratio within 5 points of NRB's ceiling. At a credit peak, a bank lending much faster than the system scores 0 on loan growth.
The interest rate banks charge each other for very short loans. When it shoots up, banks are short of money: an early sign of tightening.
NRB's band for short-term rates, with a floor (where banks can park spare money with NRB) and a ceiling (where they can borrow from NRB). The policy rate sits inside it.
example: Like the banks of a river that keep the water within a channel.

definition: Spare money in the banking system that banks have not lent out. Plenty of it pushes rates down and often lifts share prices.
A bank's benchmark lending rate, worked out from its cost of funds and other costs. Loan rates are set as the base rate plus a premium.
Money sent home by Nepalis working abroad. It is one of Nepal's largest sources of foreign money and a major source of bank deposits, so it feeds the credit cycle.
A record of all money flowing into and out of Nepal: trade, remittances, aid, investment. A surplus usually adds to bank liquidity; a deficit drains it.
The foreign currency NRB holds to pay for imports and defend the rupee. Months of import cover is the usual way to judge whether they are enough.
The Nepali rupee is fixed to the Indian rupee at 1.6 NPR per INR. It makes India's economy and interest rates matter a great deal for Nepal.
The general rise in prices. NRB put consumer inflation at 3.08% in FY 2025/26. Growth figures in the book are in rupees (nominal), not adjusted for inflation.
example: A shopkeeper whose sales rise 10% while prices rise 8% is selling only a little more rice.

definition: Nominal figures are in plain rupees; real figures remove inflation. 10% revenue growth with 3% inflation is about 6.8% real growth.
Nepal's financial year runs from 1 Shrawan to the end of Asar, roughly mid-July to mid-July. FY 2082/83 ended in mid-July 2026.
Nepali companies report at the ends of Asoj (mid-October), Poush (mid-January), Chaitra (mid-April) and Asar (mid-July, the year-end).
Nepal's official calendar, about 56 years and 8 months ahead of the international (AD) calendar. Mangsir 2083 falls in November–December 2026.
Nepal's units for large numbers. One lakh = 100,000. One crore = 10 million (100 lakh). One arba = 1 billion (100 crore). One kharba = 100 billion (100 arba).
example: A profit of Rs 2.4 arba is Rs 2.4 billion.

definition: NRB's monthly report on the economy and the banking system: deposits, lending, interest rates, NPLs, capital and more. It is the main data source for reading the money season.
NRB's umbrella term for the lenders it licenses: commercial banks, development banks, finance companies and microfinance institutions.

full: Class A, B, C and D
definition: NRB's four licence classes: A = commercial banks, B = development banks, C = finance companies, D = microfinance institutions. Each class has its own capital rules, so always compare a lender with its own class.

A lender's own capital as a share of its risk-weighted assets (mainly loans). For commercial banks NRB requires 11% total, 8.5% Tier 1 and 7% common equity, including a 2.5-point conservation buffer. NRB's figure for all 20 commercial banks together was 12.19% in mid-October 2026.
example: Like the spare tyre a bus must carry: not because it will be needed today, but because being caught without one is severe.

definition: A bank's strongest capital: share capital, retained profits and reserves that can absorb losses while the bank keeps running. Commercial banks need at least 6% plus the 2.5-point buffer, so 8.5% in all.
The purest part of Tier 1: the shareholders' own money and retained profits. Commercial banks need 4.5% plus the 2.5-point buffer, so 7% in all.
Weaker capital, such as subordinated debt and some loan-loss provisions, that helps absorb losses only after Tier 1. It counts toward total CAR.

An extra 2.5 points of common equity on top of a bank's base minimum. A bank that dips into it has not failed, but NRB limits its dividends and bonuses. The Canon treats a bank below the full 11% / 8.5% / 7% as below its minimum (a Canon rule).
example: The last few metres of water in a reservoir: you may draw on it in a drought, but you must stop handing it out.

definition: Extra capital NRB can require (up to 2.5%) in boom years, to be released in bad years. It is set at 0% for FY 2082/83.
A bank's loans and other assets, each weighted by how risky it is. A home loan counts for less than an unsecured business loan. CAR is measured against this total.
A bank so big that its failure would shake the whole system. NRB's November 2025 framework identifies 10 such banks and asks for extra capital of 0.2–1% of risk-weighted assets from 2027.

A loan whose borrower has stopped repaying on time, and the share of all loans that are in this state. NRB's figure for all 20 commercial banks together was 5.71% in mid-October 2026. A rising NPL is one of the clearest warnings that a loan book is turning sour.
A loan whose repayment terms were changed because the borrower was struggling. It may not show as an NPL, so the Canon drops a growth row if restructured loans exceed 5% of total loans.
Money a lender sets aside from profit to cover loans it expects will not be repaid. Setting provisions too low makes profit look higher than it really is.
Loan-loss provisions as a share of bad loans. Higher coverage means a better-cushioned lender.
The NFRS method of providing for losses a lender expects, not only those already suffered. Loans are sorted into stages by how risky they have become.
Under the expected-credit-loss method, loans that are already credit-impaired: the borrower is in serious trouble. Similar in spirit to NPLs.
Profit a lender books by releasing provisions made in earlier years. If more than a quarter of a year's profit comes from write-backs or one-off gains, the Canon takes off a point.
Removing a loan from the books as unrecoverable. It lowers the NPL ratio without improving the business, so the Canon also looks at a write-off-adjusted NPL ratio.
Giving a struggling borrower a new loan to repay the old one, so the bad loan never shows as overdue.
example: Paying one credit card with another: the debt never shrinks, it just changes name.

definition: What a bank earns on its loans and investments minus what it pays on deposits and borrowing, as a percentage of its interest-earning assets. It is a bank's core profit margin.
Interest earned minus interest paid, in rupees. It is a bank's main source of income.
The average interest rate a bank pays for its money (deposits and borrowing). Nabil's was 3.09% at mid-July 2026.
The share of a bank's deposits held in current and savings accounts, which pay little interest, rather than in fixed deposits. A higher CASA usually means cheaper funding.
A bank's loans divided by its deposits (with the adjustments NRB sets). NRB's ceiling is 90%. A system near the ceiling has little room to lend more, an early sign of tightening.
A large deposit from a company or organisation. It can be withdrawn in one go, so a bank that relies on them has less stable funding.
Operating costs as a share of operating income. Lower means a more efficient bank.
NRB's limit on how much a bank may lend to one borrower or connected group, to stop one failure sinking the bank.
Lending NRB requires banks to direct to low-income and disadvantaged groups, often through microfinance institutions.
A reserve NRB requires lenders to keep from profit for items such as accrued interest not yet received. It cannot be paid out as dividends.
A reserve banks must build from profit: at least 20% of each year's net profit until it equals twice the paid-up capital, then at least 10% a year (BAFIA 2073, Section 44).
Profit left for owners after the reserves the law requires. For a bank, NRB sets how it is worked out. It can be far below net profit, and it is the right base for the payout ratio.
NRB's ladder of steps for a lender whose capital falls too low: limits on lending, dividends and expansion, rising with the size of the shortfall.
A status NRB can declare for a lender in serious trouble, after which it can take over the lender's management. In the Canon Score it caps the total at 54.
Two companies combining into one. Many Nepali BFIs merged after NRB raised capital requirements. When comparing growth, a merger means part of the growth was bought, not earned.
A lender that gives small loans, often to rural women in groups, without collateral. Over-indebted borrowers and rising bad loans hit many Nepali MFIs from 2021 to 2026.
MFI loans made to members of a small group who guarantee each other. Group pressure replaces collateral.
The same borrower holding loans from several MFIs at once, often without any lender seeing the whole debt.
example: A household borrowing from three village cooperatives to cover one shortfall: each lender thinks the debt looks manageable.

definition: Taking a new loan mainly to repay an old one, not to fund real income. It keeps repayment records clean while the borrower sinks deeper.
When a borrower owes more than income can repay. It was the root of the 2021–2026 microfinance stress.
The share of an MFI's loans with any payment more than 30 days late. It warns of trouble earlier than the NPL ratio.
Loans an MFI takes from banks to fund its own lending. Heavy reliance makes it sensitive to bank interest rates.
Ratios that show how healthy a lender's loans are: NPL ratio, provision coverage, restructured loans and similar.

The long-term contract under which a buyer, usually NEA, agrees to buy a plant's electricity at set prices for a set number of years. It is the most important document for valuing a hydropower share, though river flows, transmission and how promptly NEA pays still matter.
The state-owned utility that buys almost all the power private plants produce, runs much of the grid and sells electricity to consumers.
A privately owned power company, such as most listed hydropower firms, that sells electricity to NEA under a PPA.
A plant that uses the river's flow as it comes, with little or no storage. Output is high in the monsoon and low in the dry season.
A plant that can hold water back (in a pond or reservoir) to generate when demand is highest, usually earning a better price.
The day a hydropower plant starts selling power under its PPA. Revenue begins and loan repayment starts; a late COD pushes revenue back while interest keeps adding up.
The date by which the PPA expects a plant to start selling power. Missing it can bring penalties; delays caused by the buyer's side (such as a missing transmission line) may count as a 'deemed' COD.
The amount of electricity the PPA expects a plant to deliver each year or season. The Canon's hydropower moat test asks for at least 90% of it in 2 of the last 3 years.
Actual electricity produced as a share of what the plant would produce running at full power all year.
Nepal's rivers run low in the dry months and high in the monsoon, so a plant's output, and often its tariff, differ by season. Compare the same quarter year on year.
A fixed yearly rise in the PPA price for a set number of years after COD. When the escalations end, revenue flattens.
Fees a hydropower company pays the government: one based on installed capacity and one on energy sold. Royalties usually step up after 15 years of operation, which lowers profit that year.
example: A staircase: the rent goes up on a known date.

definition: A period of no or reduced income tax for a newly commissioned plant. When it ends, profit after tax falls even if the plant runs exactly as before.
The government licence to build and run a plant for a fixed number of years. A plant with a limited licensed life should not be valued as if its cash lasts forever.
example: Like valuing a shop on a 30-year lease: count the years you can trade.

definition: Money spent on a plant that is not finished yet. It sits on the balance sheet until COD, when it becomes a working asset.
Interest on construction loans added to the project's cost instead of being shown as an expense. The company still owes it: work out interest cover using all interest, including this part.
Funding a single project mostly with loans repaid only from that project's own cash, usually through a separate company (an SPV).
A project loan that lenders can recover only from the project, not from the owners' other assets.
A company set up to own one project, keeping its debts and risks separate from the owners' other businesses.
Cash available to pay lenders ÷ the principal and interest due that year. Below 1, the project cannot meet its loan payments from its own cash. Interest cover alone misses the repayments.

full: Cash flow available for debt service
definition: The cash a project has left, after running costs and tax, to pay its lenders. It is the top line of the DSCR.
A cash reserve, often several months of loan payments, that lenders require a project to keep for bad years.
The order in which a project's cash is used: running costs, then lenders, then reserves, and only then shareholders.
example: Water fills the top pool first; only the overflow reaches the bottom.

definition: Estimates of yearly energy output: P50 is the level expected to be beaten in half of years; P90, a more cautious level, is beaten in 9 years out of 10.
The study of a river's flows over the years. It decides how much energy a plant can realistically produce.
When a plant cannot sell all the power it could produce, for example because the transmission line is full or demand is low. Whether the PPA pays for 'deemed energy' in that case matters a lot.
A project costing more than planned, often with a delay. Extra cost usually means extra debt and interest, and lower returns for shareholders.
The average cost of producing each unit of electricity over a plant's whole life, including building it. A plant whose tariff is below its LCOE loses money over its life.

Almost every listed plant sells all its power to NEA, so under the Canon's concentration table it scores 0 of 7. This is a deliberate, provisional rule: compare hydropower scores only with other hydropower scores.
The regulator for insurers in Nepal. It sets solvency, reserving and investment rules.
A company that sells life, endowment and similar policies. It collects premiums now and pays claims years or decades later, so its profit depends heavily on actuarial assumptions.
A company that insures motor, property, health, travel and similar risks, usually for one year at a time. A bad year shows quickly in its combined ratio.
Insurance for insurers: an insurer passes part of its risk, and part of the premium, to a reinsurer. Nepal has listed reinsurers, which carry other insurers' biggest risks.

full: Gross written and net earned premium
definition: The price a customer pays for a policy. Gross written premium is all policies sold in the year; net earned premium is the part kept after reinsurance and earned for cover already given. The Canon uses net earned premium as an insurer's revenue.
Claims paid and owed ÷ premiums earned. The higher it is, the less is left from each rupee of premium.
A non-life insurer's claims plus expenses, divided by premiums earned. Above 100% means it loses money on the insurance itself and relies on investment income.
Premiums earned minus claims and costs: what an insurer makes from insurance itself, before investment income.
An insurer's available capital divided by the capital it must hold for its risks. NIA's ladder sets lines at 130% (supervisory target), 100%, 70% and 45%. Under 100% caps the Canon Score at 54.
example: Like warning lines on a river gauge: each level brings stronger action.

definition: NIA's rulebook that ties the capital an insurer must hold to the risks it carries. It is being phased in, with full application from mid-July 2027.
A life insurer's net assets plus the value of profits expected from policies already sold. It shows value that yearly profit hides.
The share of a life insurer's policies that stay in force year after year. Low persistency means customers drop out early and the profit expected from them is lost.
A specialist who estimates how much money an insurer must hold today to pay future claims, using assumptions about deaths, lapses and interest.
Money an insurer holds to pay claims it owes or expects to owe. They are not ordinary debt, which is why insurers get their own capital test.
Claims for events that have already happened but have not been reported to the insurer yet. An insurer must reserve for them.
The accounting standard for insurance contracts. It spreads profit over the life of a policy through the contractual service margin.
Under NFRS 17, the profit an insurer expects from policies already sold but not yet earned. It is released into profit as cover is given.
A company's yearly book of audited accounts, auditor's report, directors' report and notes. Most of the Canon Score is built from it.
Unaudited results published each quarter on NEPSE and the company's website. First-reported figures are often revised at audit, so compare them later.
Nepal's accounting rules, based on the international IFRS standards, used by listed companies to prepare their accounts.
The individual standards within Nepal's accounting framework, such as NAS 33 on earnings per share.

full: Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal
definition: The professional body for chartered accountants and auditors in Nepal.
A snapshot of what a company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and what is left for owners (equity) on one date.
example: A photo of the household on one day: land, gold and cash, minus loans.

definition: What a company earned and spent over a period, ending in its profit or loss.
example: A month's household diary: income in, costs out, savings left.

definition: Where cash actually came from and went over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities. Profit can be on paper; cash is harder to fake.
Cash generated by the company's normal business. Investing cash flow (CFI) covers buying and selling assets; financing cash flow (CFF) covers loans, share issues and dividends.
Assets are what a company owns or is owed (cash, loans given, plant, investments). Liabilities are what it owes (deposits, borrowings, unpaid bills).
Assets minus liabilities: the owners' share of the company. Paid-up capital plus reserves and retained profit.
Profits and gains kept in the company rather than paid out, held under different headings: general reserve, share premium, revaluation reserve, retained earnings and others.
Profits the company has kept over the years instead of paying out as dividends.
The amount investors paid above face value when the company issued shares.
A paper gain from revaluing assets such as land upward. It is not cash and not profit from the business.
Money earned from the company's main business before costs. The Canon's growth test uses operating revenue only, leaving out one-off and revaluation gains.
What is left after all costs, interest and tax. For EPS and ROE, use the profit that belongs to ordinary shareholders.
Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset, such as a turbine or a building, over its useful years. It reduces profit but is not cash leaving that year.
Money spent on long-lived assets: new machines, plants, buildings.
Money tied up in running the business day to day: stock and money owed by customers, minus money owed to suppliers. When it grows, cash is absorbed.
How many days cash is tied up from buying raw materials to collecting payment from customers.
Money customers owe the company. Receivables growing much faster than sales is a red flag.
example: A shop's credit book: sales on paper, cash not yet in the drawer.

definition: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods the company holds.
A possible debt that depends on a future event, such as a court case or a guarantee. It is disclosed in the notes, not always on the balance sheet.
The extra paid above the value of net assets when buying another company. It has no value if the company is wound up.
Writing down an asset whose value has fallen below its book value, such as a loan unlikely to be repaid.
Gains and losses, such as changes in the value of some investments, that bypass the profit line and go straight to equity.
Results broken down by business line or region. It shows where profit really comes from.
Changing figures already published for an earlier year, usually to correct them. In Chapter 64 it lowers the audit check to 3 of 5.
The auditor's formal verdict on whether the accounts are fair. Read the heading the auditor uses: clean, emphasis of matter, qualified, adverse, or disclaimer.
The auditor finds the accounts fair. It is reasonable assurance, not a guarantee against fraud.
A paragraph in which the auditor points to something worth noticing while still calling the accounts fair. Scores 4 of 5 in Chapter 64.
The accounts are fair except for a specific problem. A qualification on loans, provisions or related-party dealings scores 1 and caps the Canon Score at 54.
The auditor says the accounts are not fair. Scores 0 and caps the Canon Score at 54.
The auditor could not form an opinion at all, usually because it could not get enough evidence. Scores 0 and caps the Canon Score at 54.

full: Material uncertainty related to going concern
definition: A separate section in which the auditor says there is real doubt the company can keep operating. It scores 1 and caps the Canon Score at 54.
Areas the auditor judged most significant in the audit, such as loan provisions at a bank. They are not criticisms, but they show where the risks lie.
Warning signs in the accounts that deserve a closer look: receivables racing ahead of sales, large related-party deals, frequent auditor changes, profit without cash.
Operating cash flow over three years ÷ net profit over the same three years. Below 0.5, the Canon takes off a point for a non-financial company.
example: A shop's credit book full of customers who never pay.

definition: Tax on the profit from selling shares. For resident individuals on listed shares since 22 September 2026: 3.75% if held more than 365 days, 5% if held 365 days or less.
How long you held a share before selling. Crossing 365 days lowers the capital gains tax rate.
For capital gains tax, the average price you paid for all your shares of one company, which sets your taxable gain. Not the same as WACC, the weighted average cost of capital in valuation.
Tax taken at source before you receive the money. For individuals it is final: 5% on dividends and 6% on bank interest and debenture coupons for FY 2083/84.
Selling a share at a loss to offset gains for tax, where the rules allow it. Check Chapter 38 for what Nepal's rules permit.
Your tax identification number, needed for many investment accounts and tax filings.

Net profit belonging to ordinary shareholders ÷ the weighted average number of shares. After a bonus issue EPS falls, because the same profit is shared across more shares, so compare on the same share count.
The number of shares counted only for the months they existed in the year. It is the denominator for EPS.
Share price ÷ EPS: how many years of today's profit you pay for. Compare it with the sector median, not a fixed number; a low P/E on collapsing profit is not cheap.
example: A share at Rs 600 earning Rs 40 a year has a P/E of 15.

definition: Share price ÷ book value per share: how much you pay for each rupee of net assets. Works best for banks.
example: A P/B of 2 means you pay Rs 2 for every Rs 1 of net assets.

definition: Assets minus liabilities, divided by the number of shares. A starting point for value, not a finish line.
Book value without goodwill and other intangible assets that would be worth nothing in a wind-up.
Yearly profit ÷ the shareholders' own money in the company. Use the average of opening and closing equity, and a three-year average. High ROE from heavy borrowing or thin provisions is not quality.
example: Put Rs 10 lakh into a tea shop that earns Rs 1.5 lakh a year: ROE is 15%.

definition: Profit ÷ total assets. For banks it is small (around 1–2%) because they run on borrowed money; leverage lifts ROE without lifting ROA.
Cash dividend per share ÷ share price. A 20% dividend on a Rs 100 face-value share is Rs 20; at a price of Rs 500 the yield is 4%.
Cash dividends ÷ distributable profit (the Canon's definition), counting cash only. The book prefers 30–70%, a Canon preference, not a rule of finance. Bonus shares are recorded separately.
How much a company has borrowed for every rupee of its owners' money. Chapter 64 gives 3 points under 1×, 2 at 1–2×, 1 at 2–3×, 0 at 3× or more.
Operating profit ÷ interest: how many times over the company could pay its interest. Chapter 64 gives 4 points at 5× or more (or no debt), 3 at 3–5×, 1 at 1.5–3×, 0 below 1.5×.

full: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation
definition: Operating profit before non-cash charges and financing costs. Useful for comparing companies with different debt levels.
Enterprise value (market cap plus net debt) ÷ EBITDA. It compares the whole business's value with its operating earnings; not used for banks.
The steady yearly rate that takes a starting figure to an ending figure: (end ÷ start)^(1/years) − 1.
example: Revenue from Rs 100 crore to Rs 201 crore in five years is about 14.98% a year.

definition: The middle company when all comparable companies are lined up, so one extreme company cannot drag the comparison. The Canon needs at least five peers; with fewer, the part is unverified.
The similar companies a share is compared with: operating hydropower plants only, life and non-life insurers kept apart, banks with banks.
Valuing a share by comparing its ratios (P/E, P/B) with similar companies. It tells you whether a share is cheap compared with its neighbours, not what it is worth.
example: Comparing the price of your orchard with the one next door.

definition: What a business's future cash is worth today, as opposed to its market price.
example: Counting the mangoes your trees will give over the years, not checking what the neighbour sold his orchard for.

definition: The gap between your estimate of value and the price you pay, as a share of the value. If value is Rs 54 and you pay Rs 40, the margin is about 26%.
example: A bridge built to carry three times its expected load.

definition: Valuing a business by forecasting the cash it will produce and turning future rupees into today's rupees with a discount rate. Treat the answer as a range, never one exact price.
Valuing a share from the dividends it is expected to pay, discounted to today. It suits steady dividend payers such as banks.
A simple formula for a stream of cash growing at a steady rate forever: next year's cash ÷ (required return − growth). It only works when growth is below the required return.
Cash left for owners: net profit + depreciation − capital spending − increase in working capital + new borrowing − loan repayments.
example: Net profit 10, depreciation 4, capex 3, working capital up 1, new loans 2, repayments 5: FCFE = Rs 7 crore.

full: Free cash flow to the firm
definition: Cash available to both lenders and owners, before interest and loan flows. It is discounted at WACC; never use it for banks, whose deposits are raw material, not ordinary debt.
Cash from operations minus the capital spending needed to keep and grow the business.
The yearly return you need to justify a risk. It shrinks future cash to today's value: the higher the risk, the higher the rate.

The yearly return shareholders need for the risk of owning a share. In Nepal it is usually in the low-to-mid teens; the book's examples use 12% for banks and 14.5% for hydropower. Compare ROE with it, not with the deposit rate.
The interest rate a company pays on its borrowing, after the tax saving on interest.
The blended cost of a company's debt and equity, weighted by how much of each it uses. Used to discount FCFF. (Not the same as WACC for capital gains tax.)
The return on a near-riskless investment, usually a government bond or treasury bill. It is the floor for every other required return.
The extra return investors need for owning shares instead of risk-free bonds. Nepal also adds a country risk premium.
Extra return investors need for the risks of investing in a particular country, such as currency, political and market-access risks.
How much a share tends to move with the whole market. A beta of 1.2 means it tends to rise or fall 20% more than the market.
A formula for the cost of equity: risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium. In a thin market like NEPSE, its inputs need care.

The value of all cash flows after the forecast years. It often makes up most of a DCF value, so a small change in the growth guess moves the answer a lot. For a limited-life asset such as a hydropower licence, value the remaining life instead of growth forever.
Working backwards from today's price to the growth it assumes, then asking whether that growth is believable. HHPL at Rs 85 needs about 8.7% growth a year forever.
The P/B a bank's ROE can support: (ROE − g) ÷ (cost of equity − g). A 13% ROE, 5% growth and a 12% cost of equity justify about 1.1× book.
The P/E that a company's payout, growth and cost of equity can support, from the dividend discount model.
Changing one assumption at a time (growth, discount rate) to see how much the value moves. HHPL's value ranges from about Rs 41 to Rs 83 across reasonable inputs.
What a future rupee is worth today. A rupee received in five years is worth less than a rupee now, because today's rupee can earn a return meanwhile.
A share that looks cheap on its ratios but stays cheap, or gets cheaper, because the business is weak.
example: A cheap plot of land that floods every monsoon.

definition: The P/E of the whole market. NEPSE traded at about 38 times earnings on 28 October 2025, against a historical average near 31.

This book's 100-point score for a NEPSE company, reported as Business Quality (75) + Share Attractiveness (25). It is a structured judgement on one date, never a price forecast and never an instruction to buy.
The part of the Canon Score that asks 'is this a good company?': Financial Strength (20) + Governance (15) + Durability (15) + Growth (15) + Dividends (10).
example: The house itself: walls, roof, neighbourhood.

definition: The part of the Canon Score that asks 'is the share a good buy today?': Liquidity (10) + Valuation (15).
example: The deal: can you resell easily, and is the asking price fair?

full: Old name for the score's two halves
definition: Earlier versions of the book split the score into two 'hemispheres'. Since rubric 1.6 the split is Business Quality (75) and Share Attractiveness (25); use those names.
The seven parts of the Canon Score: Financial Strength (20), Governance (15), Liquidity (10), Valuation (15), Durability (15), Growth (15) and Dividends (10).
ROE (8) + capital or leverage cushion (7) + earnings quality (5).
Chapter 64's 5-point check on whether profit is steady and real: five years of comparisons, minus a point if the cash, lender or insurer profit check fails.
Promoter holding and pledging (6) + audit opinion and related-party dealings (5) + disclosure and board (4).
Chapter 23's six-row scorecard gives a first reading and a grade. The Canon Score's governance dimension scores the evidence differently; never convert one into the other.
Average daily turnover over six months (5) + free float (5). A first screen of tradability, not proof you can sell your own order in a panic.
P/E (8) + P/B (7), each against the sector median. A cheap share gets the top row only if the discount is earned.
Moat (8) + concentration (7): will the business still matter and still earn in ten years?
Business growth (8) + EPS growth (7). For lenders, loan growth is compared with the whole system; much faster is a warning, not a strength.
example: A bus on a crowded highway: the safe speed is the speed of the traffic.

definition: Dividend record (6) + source and reason (4). Only real cash dividends count as paid.
Whatever keeps competitors from eating into profits. A licence alone is not a moat: it earns 5 of 8. The full 8 needs proof, such as ROE at or above the sector median in 4 of the last 5 years.
example: The water ditch around a fort.

definition: How much depends on one customer, product, region or supplier; for a lender, the largest share of its loan book in one sector. 20% or less earns 7 of 7; over 60% earns 0.
example: A farmer who grows one crop and sells to one trader.

full: Exceptional, Strong, Adequate, Watch list, Avoid
definition: The Canon Score's five bands: 85–100 Exceptional, 70–84 Strong, 55–69 Adequate, 45–54 Watch list, below 45 Avoid. 55 or more makes a company eligible for new money, never an instruction to buy.

Conditions that cap the whole score at 54, below the 55 needed for new money: governance under 5 of 15, the pledging check at 0, the audit check at 1 or less, NRB 'problematic' status, capital below the minimum in any layer, insurer solvency under 100%, or fraud. However many fire, it is one cap, and it lifts when the problem clears.
A Strong or Exceptional total drops one band if Business Quality is under 38 of 75 or Share Attractiveness is under 13 of 25.

A share at 0.8× its sector median or less gets the top valuation row only if its ROE is at or above the sector median (and, for a lender, its NPL at or below its class average). Otherwise it scores 'in line'.
example: Cheap is often cheap for a reason.

definition: A letter beside every score showing how many points rest on unverified or estimated figures: A none, B 1–10, C 11–20, D more than 20. Grade D means provisional.
example: Like a weather forecast that says how sure it is.

definition: A score with more than 20 points unverified (grade D). It lowers the position ceiling by one band.
A part of the score that cannot be checked from reliable sources. It may score no higher than the middle row, and its points count toward the evidence grade.
A rule that is this book's own reasoned choice, not a law or regulation, and not yet proven to give better returns. The book labels these separately from facts.
The numbered edition of the Canon Score's rules. Scores made under different versions should not be compared without re-scoring.
Testing a rule on past data. Results on data the rules were written after seeing (in-sample) prove much less than results on new data (out-of-sample).
Applying the Canon Score from 17 November 2026 onward and checking results later, with the first review due in November 2027. It is the honest test of whether the score helps.
When a scoring model that worked in the past grows less reliable because the market underneath it has changed.
A list of yes/no checks to tick before every purchase. If one box cannot be ticked, do not buy yet.
A written record of why you are buying, the score and its evidence, what would prove you wrong, and what you will do then.
Nepal's securities regulator. It oversees NEPSE, licenses brokers and merchant bankers, and approves share issues.
A founder or controlling shareholder who usually holds a large block of shares and controls the board. Promoter shares are listed separately from ordinary public shares.
Shares a promoter has given as collateral for a loan. If the loan goes bad, the lender can sell them suddenly. More than 50% pledged scores 0 and caps the Canon Score at 54.
example: A family house mortgaged to a moneylender.

definition: A deal between the company and people or firms linked to its owners or directors: loans, contracts, purchases. Judge it by size and whether the terms were at arm's length.
Terms the company would give a stranger. A related-party deal at arm's length is far less worrying than one on special terms.
A board member with no link to the promoters or management. Banks must have at least one under BAFIA 2073; other public companies at least one on a board of up to seven.
A board committee that oversees the accounts and the auditor. It works best with an independent director on it.
The yearly shareholders' meeting that approves the accounts, dividends and bonus shares. The Companies Act 2063 requires it within six months after the year ends.
Trading on important information that ordinary investors do not have yet, such as a promoter selling just before bad results. It is illegal.
When insiders know much more than outside investors. In a small market with family-controlled companies, the gap is wide.
Companies owning shares in each other, often within one business house. It can hide who really controls what and move risk around a group.
A family or group that controls several companies, often across banks, insurers and industry. Common in Nepal; watch for related-party dealings within the group.
Nepal's main company law (2006 AD): boards, AGMs, independent directors and shareholder rights.
The law governing NEPSE, SEBON, share issues and insider trading (2007 AD).
The law governing banks and financial institutions, including reserve rules and board requirements.
nepali: बैंक तथा वित्तीय संस्था सम्बन्धी ऐन, २०७३

definition: NRB's single rulebook for banks and financial institutions, reissued each year (Unified Directive 2082 is current in the book). Directive No. 1 covers capital.
Regulators' test of whether directors and senior managers are honest and competent enough to run a regulated company.
A shareholder without control, such as an ordinary retail investor. Good governance protects minority shareholders from the controlling group.
Changing auditors after a set number of years. Frequent unexplained changes, or 'opinion shopping' for a friendlier auditor, are red flags.
How you divide your money between shares, mutual funds, fixed deposits, bonds and other assets. It matters more than which single share you pick.
The share money you put into a diversified mutual fund every month through a SIP, whatever the market does. This book suggests at least half while you are learning.
example: The kitchen garden you plant every season.

definition: The share money you use for individual shares you choose yourself. How much you use depends on the money season.
example: The rented fields: how many you rent depends on the monsoon.

definition: About six months of household costs kept in a bank account or fixed deposit, so you never have to sell shares in a hurry. Keep more if your income is irregular.
example: A farmer never eats his seed rice, even in a hungry month.

definition: Spreading money across companies and sectors so one failure cannot sink you. In NEPSE, companies in one sector often fall together, so spread across sectors, not just names.
example: Not planting all your land with one crop.

definition: How closely two shares move together. Ten banks are not ten separate bets if they all rise and fall with the same credit cycle.
The most you may hold in one share by band: Exceptional 6–8% (8% is the absolute maximum), Strong 4–6%, Adequate 1.5–3%, Watch list and Avoid nothing new. They are ceilings, not targets.
Keep any one sector to about 25–30% of your share money, counting what your mutual funds hold too.
Your real exposure to a sector or company, counting your mutual funds' holdings as well as your own shares.
example: A fund holding 40% banks plus two banks of your own: your bank exposure is the two added together.

definition: Splitting a purchase into two or three buys over a few weeks, so one day's price does not decide everything. It spreads timing risk; it does not add return.
Bringing your portfolio back to its planned mix after prices have moved it away, for example by trimming a sector that has grown too large.
How far your portfolio has fallen from its recent peak, as a percentage. A 30% drawdown means it is worth 30% less than at its high.
Pre-set portfolio-level rules for what you do after given losses, written down before you need them.
Rules, written before buying, for when you will sell: why you bought, what would prove you wrong, and what you will do then.
example: A farmer decides when to harvest before the season starts, so the first hailstorm does not panic him.

definition: One or two lines on why you are buying a share, with the evidence that would prove it wrong.
Your own written rulebook for investing: goals, limits, process and what you will never do.
Going against your score or rules. This book allows it only for a documented company event, never for a mood or a rumour.
Checking how long you would take to sell if turnover fell sharply, for example to a quarter of normal. If the answer is longer than you could bear, hold less.
A return measure that accounts for money added and withdrawn on irregular dates. It is the honest way to measure a real portfolio with IPOs, rights and top-ups.
A yardstick to compare your returns with, such as the NEPSE index or a simple mutual-fund SIP.
Buying good businesses at prices below their worth, and holding patiently.
Buying because everyone else is, from fear of missing out. It drove much of the 2021 NEPSE mania.
Fixing on a number, often the price you paid, and judging everything against it. Your purchase price is not a reason to hold.
Feeling a loss about twice as strongly as a gain of the same size, which tempts you to hold losers too long.
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long.
Looking only for information that agrees with what you already believe.
Believing your knowledge or timing is better than it is, which leads to trading too often and holding too little in reserve.
